page_review.word_count_method: Whitespace-delimited tokens extracted from owned pages 174-196 after removing running heads, source page numbers, and chapter-title wording; substantive chapter body text and block quotations retained. Context pages were reviewed but excluded from the count.

excluded_regions.role: running furniture and source page numbers
chapter-title wording excluded from the source-word denominator; the title remains unit metadata and an access concept

unavailable_regions.reason: Absent from the supplied special edition. Superscript note markers remain in body text, but note text is unavailable and excluded from discovery.

selection_method.unit: independently searchable source subject rather than proposed index heading
principles: Retain principal subjects and significant localized or subsidiary subjects even when confined to one passage.
Split subjects when a reader could plausibly seek one without the other or when a combined label would overstate page support.
Retain named people, institutions, works, and events only when the chapter analyzes them, uses them as sustained explanatory cases, or makes them independently useful to scholarly readers.
Preserve qualifications, reported beliefs, disputed causation, and the author's degree of commitment.
Use optional only for defensible supplemental access whose absence would not materially reduce usefulness.
Do not use density calibration to set the subject count or priority.
Complete the fresh source-led inventory before consulting prior chapter artifacts for schema and procedural consistency.

reader_tasks.prompt: Trace how constitutional monarchy moved from the October 1791 accommodation to suspension on 10 August 1792.
Explain why Brissotins, the royal family, generals, and other deputies supported war for incompatible reasons.
Compare Brissot's regenerative case for war with Robespierre's warnings about dictatorship, defeat, and domestic enemies.
Follow the refractory-priest problem from the Assembly's opening priorities through veto conflict and post-10 August deportation.
Explain how the Saint-Domingue uprising connected colonial policy, slavery, Bordeaux interests, sugar scarcity, and Parisian price-fixing.
Connect currency decline, provisioning, and grain or sugar unrest to revived popular organization.
Explain the causes and meaning assigned to southern anti-feudal violence in spring 1792.
Trace the organizational path from popular societies and 20 June through federes, democratized sections, and the 10 August insurrection.
Explain how the Brunswick Manifesto and military reverses accelerated democratization and deposition demands.
Identify how power shifted from the Legislative Assembly to the insurrectionary Commune after 10 August.
Reconstruct the causes, actors, victims, scale, and political afterlife of the September Massacres without treating most victims as genuine counter-revolutionaries.
Explain the relationship between invasion panic, internal repression, volunteering, and Valmy.
Describe how the Convention was elected, who served in it, and why political continuity remained high despite broad male suffrage.
Trace the emerging Girondin-Montagnard division from conflict over the Commune through the appeal-to-the-people debate.
Reconstruct the legal arguments, four roll calls, execution, and consequences of the trial of Louis XVI.

subjects.label: The Republican Revolution, October 1791-January 1793
subjects.meaning: The chapter's governing transformation from constitutional monarchy through war and popular insurrection to republic and regicide.
subjects.stance: The transformation is an irreversible rupture, but its regicidal climax is presented as a dangerous challenge rather than an uncomplicated victory.

target_labels: Collapse of constitutional monarchy
Insurrection of 10 August 1792 and assault on the Tuileries
Abolition of monarchy and establishment of the Republic
Execution of Louis XVI and regicide

evidence.evidence_summary: The chapter opens with a new legislature shaped by post-1789 local experience and hostility toward perceived domestic enemies.
The failed June confrontation and preparations for another make the constitutional settlement appear exhausted.
The 10 August victory suspends monarchy and transfers effective power away from the legislature.
Valmy coincides with the Convention's meeting and immediate declaration of a republic.
The king's execution is interpreted as completing the break with the old order while escalating opposition.

subjects.label: Legislative Assembly: composition, experience, and priorities
subjects.meaning: The 745 deputies were predominantly propertied lawyers whose local revolutionary service gave them substantial practical experience.
subjects.stance: The text corrects the departing Constituent deputies' view that the new legislators were obscure and callow; local office had taught them both administration and suspicion of domestic enemies.

target_labels: Refractory/non-juring priests as a political crisis
Emigres: emigration, decrees, and war pretext

evidence.evidence_summary: The Assembly's social composition, local prominence, and practical experience in guards, clubs, courts, and administration are analyzed.
Clerical resistance and emigration are identified as the deputies' most urgent opening problems.

subjects.label: Legislative Assembly: declining authority and subordination to the Commune
subjects.meaning: By August 1792 the Assembly could neither control insurrection nor command a full attendance, and its remaining deputies largely complied with the new Commune.
subjects.stance: The decline is not treated as a single formal surrender; it emerges from indecision, absenteeism, and the superior mobilizing power of the sections and Commune.

target_labels: Insurrection of 10 August 1792 and assault on the Tuileries
Insurrectionary Paris Commune

evidence.evidence_summary: Deposition and Lafayette questions move beyond the deputies' ability to manage them.
The Assembly watches the decisive confrontation and then suspends monarchy under insurrectionary pressure.
Fewer than three hundred deputies make appointments, and the rump usually follows Commune demands.

subjects.label: Collapse of constitutional monarchy
subjects.meaning: The constitutional experiment disintegrated through royal vetoes, war, ministerial conflict, popular pressure, and finally armed overthrow.
subjects.stance: The monarchy's fall is cumulative: neither the king's legal constitutional powers nor the demonstrators' early failures preserved trust or authority.

target_labels: The Republican Revolution, October 1791-January 1793
Insurrection of 10 August 1792 and assault on the Tuileries

evidence.evidence_summary: A brief accommodation joins royal gestures, Feuillant advice, and initial legislative cooperation.
The emigre veto ends the early honeymoon and revives suspicions of palace conspiracy.
Military reverses and new veto conflicts produce a ministerial and security crisis.
The failed 20 June invasion demonstrates both popular hostility and the king's remaining personal resolve.
The fall of the Tuileries destroys royal authority and results in suspension of monarchy.

subjects.label: Royal veto as constitutional and political crisis
subjects.meaning: Louis XVI used his lawful veto against emigre, clerical, and federe measures, but opponents interpreted the pattern as protection of enemies and obstruction of national defense.
subjects.stance: The text acknowledges the veto's constitutional legitimacy while showing why its political meaning became fatal to trust.

target_labels: Collapse of constitutional monarchy
Legislative Assembly: composition, experience, and priorities

evidence.evidence_summary: The king rejects the punitive emigre decree despite having a constitutional right to do so.
His later rejection of the nonjuror decree deepens suspicions of royal sympathy with enemies.
The king plans vetoes of clerical deportation and the proposed federe camp.
Ministerial criticism of the veto delays brings the executive conflict into the open.

subjects.label: Popular sovereignty versus representative authority
subjects.meaning: Sections, the insurrectionary Commune, the Convention, and rival trial theories made competing claims to act for the sovereign people.
subjects.stance: The source does not treat popular and representative sovereignty as harmoniously aligned; each claim could undermine another institution's legitimacy.

target_labels: Paris sections and popular societies
Insurrectionary Paris Commune
National Convention: formation, elections, and composition
Trial of Louis XVI: legality and procedure

evidence.evidence_summary: Sections remove active-citizen restrictions and coordinate political action outside established representative limits.
The insurrectionary Commune compels the legislature to suspend monarchy and convoke a Convention.
The Convention is framed as a new assembly formed to secure popular sovereignty, but through a mediated electoral process.
Debate over trying the king turns on whether popular judgment was already complete or required representative procedure.

subjects.label: Democratization of citizenship and political participation
subjects.meaning: Emergency politics eroded the active-passive citizen distinction in sections, the National Guard, and Convention elections.
subjects.stance: Broader formal participation did not ensure broad turnout or eliminate institutional mediation.

target_labels: Paris sections and popular societies
National Guard: politicization and democratization
National Convention: formation, elections, and composition

evidence.evidence_summary: Sections begin admitting citizens without the former status distinction and receive authority for continuous sittings.
All defenders are treated as active citizens, opening arms and National Guard membership beyond property holders.
Convention elections use broad manhood suffrage but retain two stages and draw only a minority of eligible voters.

subjects.label: National Convention: formation, elections, and composition
subjects.meaning: The Convention arose from the 10 August settlement, was elected through a broad but indirect male franchise, and combined new social breadth with substantial political continuity.
subjects.stance: Low participation and uncertain provincial information qualify any simple claim that the Convention directly represented a fully mobilized nation.

target_labels: Legislative Assembly: declining authority and subordination to the Commune
Abolition of monarchy and establishment of the Republic

evidence.evidence_summary: Electoral rules, low turnout, and the return of many experienced deputies are analyzed.
The Convention's age, professions, property base, limited artisan presence, and revolutionary experience are described.

subjects.label: Abolition of monarchy and establishment of the Republic
subjects.meaning: The Convention abolished monarchy and established a republic immediately after meeting in September 1792.
subjects.stance: The institutional break was decisive, but it did not by itself settle the fate of Louis XVI or eliminate political conflict.

target_labels: Insurrection of 10 August 1792 and assault on the Tuileries
Trial of Louis XVI: legality and procedure

evidence.evidence_summary: The Convention's first action is to declare a republic as the Prussians retreat after Valmy.
Monarchy is formally abolished and the later revolutionary calendar dates Year I from the republican foundation.

subjects.label: Trial of Louis XVI: legality and procedure
subjects.meaning: The Convention confronted the king's former constitutional inviolability, the claim that 10 August had already judged him, and deputies' insistence on a hearing before the sovereign representatives.
subjects.stance: The verdict is presented as politically inevitable, yet legal training and procedural legitimacy still mattered to the deputies.

target_labels: Popular sovereignty versus representative authority
Execution of Louis XVI and regicide

evidence.evidence_summary: Evidence from the palace and the king's former inviolability generate arguments over whether a trial is legitimate at all.
The Convention chooses a hearing, presents an indictment, permits counsel, and debates the political meaning of procedure.

subjects.label: Execution of Louis XVI and regicide
subjects.meaning: Four Convention decisions established guilt, rejected a popular appeal, selected death over imprisonment or delay, and refused reprieve before the king's execution.
subjects.stance: The execution rested on close and politically pressured divisions, not unanimous enthusiasm for immediate death.

target_labels: Trial of Louis XVI: legality and procedure
The Republican Revolution, October 1791-January 1793

evidence.evidence_summary: Near-unanimous guilt contrasts with a large minority favoring an appeal to the people.
Closely divided punishment and reprieve votes lead to execution on 21 January 1793.

subjects.label: Consequences and meaning of regicide
subjects.meaning: Regicide made compromise and return to the old order far less possible while strengthening and multiplying the Revolution's enemies.
subjects.stance: The chapter calls regicide a logical climax but stresses that it posed a challenge whose consequences would intensify conflict in 1793.

target_labels: The Republican Revolution, October 1791-January 1793
Irreversibility of the destruction of the old order

evidence.evidence_summary: The closing synthesis presents execution as irreversible rupture that satisfies militants but generates wider domestic and European hostility.

subjects.label: Emergence of the Girondin-Montagnard conflict
subjects.meaning: Conflict over the Commune, the massacres, the king, and provincial consultation hardened Brissot's circle and the Paris deputies into rival groupings.
subjects.stance: The terminology is historically staged: the text shows a faction taking shape rather than projecting a fully organized party backward over the entire chapter.

target_labels: Brissotins/Girondins: war leadership and loss of popular control
Appeal to the people in the king's trial
Political memory and blame for the September Massacres

evidence.evidence_summary: Robespierre names a Gironde faction during the Commune's conflict with Brissot and allied ministers.
Each emerging side accuses the other of responsibility or complicity in the massacres.
Paris deputies on the high benches form the Montagnard kernel and oppose Girondin hesitation over the king.
The appeal-to-the-people proposal produces the bitterest division yet in the Convention.

subjects.label: Appeal to the people in the king's trial
subjects.meaning: Girondins proposed submitting the sentence to popular confirmation, while opponents saw a provincial rejection of death as a path to civil war.
subjects.stance: The proposal is treated as a substantive constitutional and factional issue, not merely a device for saving the king.
acceptable_access: Louis XVI, sentence and popular appeal

target_labels: Execution of Louis XVI and regicide
Emergence of the Girondin-Montagnard conflict

evidence.evidence_summary: The Girondin proposal seeks provincial confirmation amid fears that disagreement between Paris and the provinces would cause civil war.
The roll call rejects the appeal by a substantial but not overwhelming margin.

subjects.label: Sans-culotte pressure on Convention voting
subjects.meaning: Threats and rumors of renewed street and prison violence formed part of the environment in which deputies voted on the king's punishment.
subjects.stance: The source says fear may have influenced some votes; it does not claim that coercion alone determined the sentence.

target_labels: Execution of Louis XVI and regicide
Sans-culottes as a political movement

evidence.evidence_summary: Rumors that militants would attack the Temple or Convention accompany the close punishment vote and may sway some deputies.

subjects.label: Feuillants: constitutional reconciliation and political decline
subjects.meaning: The Feuillants advised royal conciliation and initially attracted many deputies, but private organization, lack of public political appeal, antiwar caution, and association with weak ministries marginalized them.
subjects.stance: Their decline is attributed to organizational and political disadvantages, not to an absence of constitutional ideas or supporters at the chapter's start.

target_labels: Jacobin Club: ascendancy and radicalization
Collapse of constitutional monarchy

evidence.evidence_summary: Feuillant leaders encourage reconciliation and initially draw far more new deputies than the Jacobins.
Private meetings and the absence of compelling public leaders cause rapid decline.
Feuillant leaders join Robespierre in warning against a wider war.
Replacement ministers are dismissed as weak Feuillant figures associated with Lafayette.

subjects.label: Jacobin Club: ascendancy and radicalization
subjects.meaning: The Jacobins' public forum, recognized leaders, and national debate displaced the Feuillants and later supported insurrectionary and factional politics.
subjects.stance: The club was not politically uniform: the war controversy sharply divided Brissot and Robespierre before it moved toward overthrow of monarchy.

target_labels: Feuillants: constitutional reconciliation and political decline
Brissot-Robespierre war controversy

evidence.evidence_summary: Ambitious deputies prefer public Jacobin sessions and access to established national figures.
The club becomes the place where nationally important questions are debated while the Feuillants fade.
Nightly debate pits Brissot's war program against Robespierre's objections.
The club increasingly supports overthrow by insurrection, with Robespierre joining the call for direct action.
The massacres become material for factional accusation within Jacobin politics.

subjects.label: Brissotins/Girondins: war leadership and loss of popular control
subjects.meaning: Brissot and allied Bordeaux deputies drove war policy and ministry formation, blamed rivals for reverses, attempted to use popular pressure, and then lost control as sections moved toward complete overthrow.
subjects.stance: The chapter distinguishes their early revolutionary initiative from their later equivocation and provincial strategy; it does not present a fixed Girondin party from the outset.

target_labels: Origins and declaration of the war of April 1792
Insurrectionary Paris Commune
Emergence of the Girondin-Montagnard conflict

evidence.evidence_summary: Brissot links punitive emigre policy to possible war and shapes the Assembly's decree.
Brissot and Bordeaux allies promote war as national regeneration and a test of the king.
A ministry largely aligned with Brissot replaces the dismissed royal ministers and clears the path to war.
Early reverses lead the war party to accuse king, generals, and palace plotters.
Girondin efforts to recover office fail as they oppose the deposition movement they helped unleash.
Their effort to disband the Commune provokes a confrontation with Robespierre and sectional power.
Girondin deputies hesitate over immediate disposal of the king.
They champion an appeal to the people and sharpen conflict with the Mountain.

subjects.label: Robespierre: antiwar case, turn to insurrection, and position on Louis XVI
subjects.meaning: Robespierre opposed the war as a route to dictatorship or counter-revolution, later endorsed direct action against monarchy, attacked the Gironde, and argued that popular victory had already condemned Louis.
subjects.stance: His positions change with circumstances but retain a focus on domestic enemies and distrust of generals and representative delay.
acceptable_access: Robespierre and trial of Louis XVI

target_labels: Brissot-Robespierre war controversy
Insurrection of 10 August 1792 and assault on the Tuileries
Saint-Just's argument that the king had already been judged

evidence.evidence_summary: He warns that victory could empower Lafayette and defeat could enable the Court and foreign forces.
He continues opposing escalation even after Austrian threats strengthen the war party.
He abandons defense of the constitution and publicly supports direct action.
He identifies a Gironde faction during conflict over the Commune.
He endorses Saint-Just's claim that the people have already judged the king.
He argues that a conventional trial risks placing the Revolution itself under judgment.

subjects.label: Lafayette: war aims, coup suspicion, political failure, and flight
subjects.meaning: Lafayette supported war as a means to restore military and domestic order, became the central object of fears of military dictatorship, failed to rally political support, and fled after 10 August.
subjects.stance: The text presents coup suspicions as politically powerful and partly grounded in his interventions, without stating that a completed coup plan existed.

target_labels: Brissot-Robespierre war controversy
Paris sections and popular societies

evidence.evidence_summary: Lafayette expects war to revive the army and enable restoration of domestic stability.
Robespierre identifies a successful Lafayette as a potential military dictator.
Security measures and military reorganization are shaped by fear of a coup associated with him.
His letter from the front denounces Jacobins and intensifies coup suspicions.
His attempt to rally the Guard and Crown fails, leaving him politically isolated.
After considering action against Paris, he crosses enemy lines and is imprisoned by Austria.

subjects.label: Danton: sectional leadership and crisis government
subjects.meaning: Danton helped democratize sectional politics, became justice minister after 10 August, restrained an attempted Commune purge, rallied resistance during invasion, and entered the Convention.
subjects.stance: He is shown as a bridge between sans-culotte power and government rather than as the sole organizer of either insurrection or massacre.

target_labels: Paris sections and popular societies
Insurrectionary Paris Commune
Legislative Assembly: declining authority and subordination to the Commune

evidence.evidence_summary: Under Danton's leadership a section rejects active-citizen restrictions and broadens participation.
He enters the ministry to connect the new government with the sans-culottes and dominates the crisis response.
He prevents arrests sought by the Commune and calls for mass volunteering as invasion advances.
His election to the Convention ends his ministerial role.

subjects.label: Petion: mayoral role in the popular-monarchical crisis
subjects.meaning: Petion's mayoralty symbolized Jacobin ascendancy; his handling of 20 June, suspension and restoration became mobilizing issues, and he later supported formal trial procedure.
subjects.stance: His movement away from Robespierre is gradual and should not be projected backward over his earlier popularity with radicals.

target_labels: Demonstration of 20 June 1792
Trial of Louis XVI: legality and procedure

evidence.evidence_summary: His decisive mayoral victory over Lafayette illustrates the appeal of prominent Jacobin figures.
He ends the palace invasion but is then publicly blamed and suspended for failing to prevent it.
His restoration becomes a demand of federes and a concession around the 14 July festival.
He presents the deposition demand in the name of the sections but is kept symbolically out of the insurrectionary seizure.
His motion secures a trial before the Convention rather than immediate punishment without hearing.

subjects.label: Roland ministry and the June ministerial crisis
subjects.meaning: Roland's Brissotin-aligned ministry helped launch war; his public rebuke of the king precipitated the June purge, and the ousted ministers' restoration became an immediate popular demand.
subjects.stance: The ministerial crisis is treated as both a constitutional conflict and a catalyst deliberately used by popular and factional actors.

target_labels: Collapse of constitutional monarchy
Demonstration of 20 June 1792

evidence.evidence_summary: Roland joins the ministry formed under Brissotin pressure before the declaration of war.
His public letter blames royal delay and results in dismissal of the principal ministers.
The fallen ministers return after 10 August, though now burdened by Girondin equivocation.

subjects.label: Dumouriez: war ministry and Valmy diplomacy
subjects.meaning: Dumouriez replaced Delessart, helped bring the declaration of war, later commanded at Valmy, and opened negotiations that briefly made an early peace possible.
subjects.stance: His patriotic performance coexisted with pragmatic diplomacy; he is not reduced to the public war rhetoric he used in Paris.

target_labels: Origins and declaration of the war of April 1792
Battle of Valmy and its political significance

evidence.evidence_summary: He becomes foreign minister, sustains war enthusiasm, and unsuccessfully explores Prussian neutrality before the declaration.
His forces join Kellermann's in outnumbering and halting the Prussians at Valmy.
He initiates negotiations after the battle, but the new Republic causes the Prussians to break them off.

subjects.label: Marat and advocacy of massacre
subjects.meaning: After 10 August Marat's call to kill imprisoned suspects and selected political leaders gained influence in Commune politics.
subjects.stance: The source records his advocacy and institutional role without making him the sole cause of the massacres.

target_labels: September Massacres
Insurrectionary Paris Commune

evidence.evidence_summary: His previously marginal demand for massacre becomes politically influential after the overthrow.
The Commune adds him to prison surveillance during its confrontation with the Assembly.
His notoriety helps secure election to the Convention.

subjects.label: Saint-Just's argument that the king had already been judged
subjects.meaning: Saint-Just argued that the people's victory on 10 August had already established guilt, leaving punishment rather than trial as the Convention's task.
subjects.stance: The argument is presented as a radical challenge to ordinary legal process and later taken up by Robespierre.

target_labels: Robespierre: antiwar case, turn to insurrection, and position on Louis XVI
Trial of Louis XVI: legality and procedure

evidence.evidence_summary: Saint-Just's first Convention speech treats 10 August as a completed popular verdict and demands punishment.

subjects.label: Marie Antoinette, secret correspondence, and the alleged Austrian Committee
subjects.meaning: Deputies interpreted royal vetoes as proof of a queen-led palace conspiracy, although her real secret correspondence sought confrontation and foreign intervention rather than protection of emigres from legislation.
subjects.stance: The alleged Austrian Committee must remain identified as suspicion or rumor; real correspondence does not validate every conspiratorial inference.

target_labels: Counter-revolution and the enemy within
Competing public and secret war aims

evidence.evidence_summary: The emigre veto is interpreted by Brissot's allies as concrete evidence of a queen-coordinated counter-revolutionary committee.
The text distinguishes extensive secret correspondence and a desire for confrontation from the deputies' specific theory about protecting emigres.
The queen's indifference to constitutional pacification contributes to Barnave's withdrawal and continued mistrust.

subjects.label: Cordeliers-centered popular coordination
subjects.meaning: Popular societies and Cordeliers networks coordinated the 20 June action and helped rebuild the organizational capacity later used for insurrection.
subjects.stance: The Cordeliers are an organizing center among multiple sections, not a substitute label for the entire popular movement.

target_labels: Demonstration of 20 June 1792
Paris sections and popular societies

evidence.evidence_summary: A radical secession and new popular leaders illustrate revived organization around Cordeliers politics.
Eastern sections coordinate their mass demonstration from the Cordeliers.

subjects.label: Refractory/non-juring priests as a political crisis
subjects.meaning: Clerical refusal of revolutionary oaths drove local repression, national decrees, royal vetoes, deportation, and widening suspicion before and after the monarchy fell.
subjects.stance: The source treats nonjuror resistance as a major political problem while also showing how the category of suspect clergy expanded beyond those originally subject to oaths.

target_labels: Legislative Assembly: composition, experience, and priorities
Counter-revolution and the enemy within

evidence.evidence_summary: Local Jacobins, guards, and officials had already supervised, exiled, or imprisoned refractory clergy before the new Assembly met.
Large-scale oath refusal in the Vendee confirms the issue's urgency.
The Assembly imposes a new oath, surveillance, possible exile, and restrictions on worship before the king vetoes the decree.
Military panic revives deportation legislation, which becomes part of another veto conflict.
After 10 August deportation expands, including clergy not originally bound by the oaths.
More than two hundred priests are among the massacre victims.

subjects.label: Vendee clerical resistance
subjects.meaning: The Vendee supplied a concentrated example of parish priests rejecting the revolutionary oath and resisting the new ecclesiastical settlement.
subjects.stance: The chapter uses the episode to demonstrate scale and urgency; it does not yet provide a full account of later Vendee rebellion.

target_labels: Refractory/non-juring priests as a political crisis

evidence.evidence_summary: Reports that most parish priests in the department refused the oath make the Vendee a leading example in the opening debate.

subjects.label: Avignon violence and annexation conflict
subjects.meaning: Reciprocal killings between opponents and supporters of French annexation made Avignon a symbol and cause of widening religious-counterrevolutionary conflict in the south.
subjects.stance: The text presents violence on both sides and does not describe annexationist action as a simple restoration of order.

target_labels: Southern peasant anti-feudal violence
Marseilles: regional radicalism and intervention

evidence.evidence_summary: A municipal killing and the retaliatory murder of imprisoned papal supporters enter the clerical debate.
The Avignon prison killings remain part of the rumor complex behind later southern violence.

subjects.label: Emigres: emigration, decrees, and war pretext
subjects.meaning: Continuing emigration, armed organization abroad, punitive legislation, royal resistance, and pressure on German rulers converted a domestic opposition problem into a route toward war.
subjects.stance: The chapter distinguishes the emigres' symbolic and political importance from Robespierre's judgment that they were less dangerous than domestic counter-revolutionaries.

target_labels: Origins and declaration of the war of April 1792
Counter-revolution and the enemy within

evidence.evidence_summary: Emigration accelerates despite amnesty, while armed activity near the frontier sustains suspicion.
The Assembly sequesters revenues and threatens absent citizens with severe penalties before the king vetoes the decree.
The Assembly redirects pressure toward German rulers harboring armed emigres.
The Trier ultimatum briefly appears to solve the immediate problem when the electors disperse emigre forces.
Austrian intervention shifts the war focus from the Rhine electors to the Habsburg ruler.

subjects.label: Counter-revolution and the enemy within
subjects.meaning: The category of internal enemies expanded from nonjurors and royalist plotters to foreigners, guards, ministers, prisoners, criminals, and other presumed conspirators.
subjects.stance: The source repeatedly exposes the gap between real opposition and indiscriminate suspicion; many targets were not demonstrably dangerous.

target_labels: Political surveillance after 10 August
Domiciliary visits, mass arrests, and prison overcrowding
September Massacres

evidence.evidence_summary: Local political experience teaches new deputies to identify refractory clergy as domestic enemies.
Royal veto is interpreted through a broad alleged palace-emigre-foreign conspiracy.
Southern rumor turns an accidental-looking disaster into evidence of a coordinated counter-revolutionary plot.
Military defeat prompts surveillance, disbandment, deportation, and claims that betrayal is everywhere.
Passports, searches, clerical arrests, and thousands of new detentions operationalize suspicion.
Most massacre victims prove not to be politically dangerous despite perpetrators' belief in a prison conspiracy.

subjects.label: Origins and declaration of the war of April 1792
subjects.meaning: Emigre politics, Austrian threats, Brissotin regeneration, royal and military hopes, diplomatic escalation, and ministerial change converged in an overwhelmingly approved declaration of war.
subjects.stance: No single motive explains the war; shared support concealed incompatible expectations about the Revolution's survival or defeat.

target_labels: Emigres: emigration, decrees, and war pretext
Austrian escalation and Austro-Prussian alignment
War as panacea and instrument of national regeneration
Competing public and secret war aims

evidence.evidence_summary: Brissot first makes war a possible final solution to the emigre problem.
The king, Lafayette, Narbonne, and Brissotins discover different advantages in confrontation.
The Assembly embraces the Trier ultimatum while Robespierre warns against war.
Austrian threats, alliance politics, and ministry conflict convert the question into direct war against the Habsburg ruler.
A Brissotin-aligned ministry is installed and the Assembly approves war with only a handful of dissenters.

subjects.label: War as panacea and instrument of national regeneration
subjects.meaning: War advocates expected conflict to restore honor, regenerate nation and army, expose traitors, spread liberty, support the currency, and redirect domestic antagonism.
subjects.stance: The chapter emphasizes the breadth and unreality of these expectations; war briefly distracted from domestic problems but did not solve them.

target_labels: Origins and declaration of the war of April 1792
Opening military collapse and the army's crisis

evidence.evidence_summary: Brissotins describe war as a way to regenerate the nation, restore honor, expose plotters, and liberate Europe.
Patriotic enthusiasm and expectations that liberated peoples will imitate France overwhelm caution.
The declared defensive war carries expansive aims and divergent hopes.
War temporarily directs attention outward, but domestic crises multiply by the time fighting begins.

subjects.label: Competing public and secret war aims
subjects.meaning: Revolutionaries publicly promised defense and liberation, while the king, queen, and generals expected defeat, intervention, restored authority, or domestic discipline.
subjects.stance: Common support for war must not be mistaken for agreement about its desired outcome; the public no-conquest and civilian-protection pledges were later broken.

target_labels: Origins and declaration of the war of April 1792
Revolutionary internationalism and liberation war

evidence.evidence_summary: The king and military leaders expect war to invite intervention or restore discipline, unlike Brissotin liberation goals.
The declaration's defensive promises are set beside the manifold and incompatible aims of factions, generals, and the royal family.

subjects.label: Brissot-Robespierre war controversy
subjects.meaning: Brissot defended war as necessary consolidation and international liberation, while Robespierre warned that victory could empower generals and defeat could enable court-led counter-revolution.
subjects.stance: The controversy is substantive rather than merely personal: it offers competing diagnoses of where the Revolution's most dangerous enemies were located.

target_labels: Brissotins/Girondins: war leadership and loss of popular control
Robespierre: antiwar case, turn to insurrection, and position on Louis XVI

evidence.evidence_summary: Robespierre identifies military dictatorship, defeat, foreign intervention, and domestic enemies as the central risks.
Brissot's optimism dominates Assembly enthusiasm while Robespierre and Feuillants remain isolated opponents.

subjects.label: Austrian escalation and Austro-Prussian alignment
subjects.meaning: Habsburg threats on behalf of the Rhine electors and a defensive pact with Prussia convinced French war advocates that a monarchical league was forming against the Revolution.
subjects.stance: Vienna believed calibrated threats would defuse crisis, but the strategy instead strengthened the French case for war.
acceptable_access: Leopold II and French war crisis

target_labels: Origins and declaration of the war of April 1792
Revolutionary internationalism and liberation war

evidence.evidence_summary: Leopold's threat and the Prussian pact reinforce the belief in a league of despots and provoke escalating French demands.
A defiant Austrian reply, ministerial collapse, and Austrian mobilization remove remaining obstacles to war.

subjects.label: Revolutionary internationalism and liberation war
subjects.meaning: War rhetoric treated French liberty as universally valid and expected subject peoples to rise with French assistance.
subjects.stance: The source stresses that claims of no conquest and protection of civilians were incompatible with the conflict's later course.

target_labels: Origins and declaration of the war of April 1792
The Marseillaise: composition and naming

evidence.evidence_summary: The Assembly threatens German rulers with the awakening of their subject peoples.
Brissotin and exile rhetoric predicts liberation throughout Europe.
Advocates interpret Habsburg action as a league of despots to be confronted directly.
The declaration promises defense without conquest, followed by the author's warning that every pledge will be broken.

subjects.label: Opening military collapse and the army's crisis
subjects.meaning: The first advance ended in panic, desertion, and the killing of a suspected commander, exposing the weakness of an army war advocates had imagined as liberating.
subjects.stance: Defeat is explained through military condition and expectation, not simply through treason despite contemporary accusations.

target_labels: War as panacea and instrument of national regeneration
Military defeat, treason panic, and domestic radicalization

evidence.evidence_summary: The first Belgian advance collapses, and French troops kill a commander they suspect of betrayal.
Other units fail, cavalry desertion increases, and Paris responds by seeking political scapegoats.

subjects.label: Military defeat, treason panic, and domestic radicalization
subjects.meaning: Defeat and invasion transformed military danger into beliefs that king, generals, clergy, foreigners, prisoners, and political rivals were betraying the nation.
subjects.stance: The source treats military emergency as a major accelerator of repression and revolution while repeatedly qualifying the truth of alleged plots.

target_labels: Opening military collapse and the army's crisis
Longwy and Verdun: invasion panic
Political surveillance after 10 August
September Massacres

evidence.evidence_summary: Opening reverses produce widespread betrayal claims and rapid security legislation.
Enemy invasion and the Brunswick threat intensify democratization and the deposition movement.
The fall of Longwy leads to searches, arrests, and prison overcrowding.
Verdun's danger triggers panic and the opening attacks on prisoners.
After the internal purge, popular volunteering and Valmy connect domestic mobilization to military recovery.

subjects.label: Brunswick Manifesto and the overthrow of monarchy
subjects.meaning: The allied commander's threat to restore royal authority and punish Paris radicalized the capital and made the king appear aligned with invasion.
subjects.stance: The manifesto's political effect in France is central; its threats backfired rather than intimidating Parisians into passivity.

target_labels: Insurrection of 10 August 1792 and assault on the Tuileries
National Guard: politicization and democratization

evidence.evidence_summary: The manifesto threatens vengeance, prompts arms for all citizens, and intensifies petitions for immediate deposition.

subjects.label: Country in Danger and emergency mobilization
subjects.meaning: The Country in Danger procedure placed public bodies in permanent session and authorized volunteer mobilization alongside the line army.
subjects.stance: Emergency mobilization was simultaneously military and political, bringing provincial militants into Paris and widening participation.

target_labels: Federes as military volunteers and political actors
Democratization of citizenship and political participation

evidence.evidence_summary: The Assembly defines and invokes the emergency, enabling permanent sessions and volunteer recruitment.
Invasion and the Brunswick threat deepen the emergency's democratizing consequences.

subjects.label: Federes as military volunteers and political actors
subjects.meaning: Provincial National Guard volunteers entered Paris en route to the front, joined deposition politics, and became an armed component of the 10 August insurrection.
subjects.stance: They were not merely military replacements; sections and clubs deliberately integrated them into the capital's political struggle.

target_labels: Country in Danger and emergency mobilization
Insurrection of 10 August 1792 and assault on the Tuileries

evidence.evidence_summary: The proposed camp of provincial guards becomes a new point of veto and political conflict.
Federes continue arriving, receive Jacobin and sectional support, and demand action against royal and military opponents.
They coordinate with the sections as insurrection approaches.
Federes march with the Commune's forces and suffer substantial casualties at the Tuileries.

subjects.label: National Guard: politicization and democratization
subjects.meaning: The Guard was a school of revolutionary administration, an object of conflict between Paris officers and provincial volunteers, and an armed institution opened beyond propertied active citizens in the invasion crisis.
subjects.stance: It should not be treated as a politically uniform body; officers, local units, and newly admitted citizens took different positions.

target_labels: Legislative Assembly: composition, experience, and priorities
Insurrection of 10 August 1792 and assault on the Tuileries

evidence.evidence_summary: Service in the Guard provided new deputies with practical revolutionary experience.
The royal guard, regular troops, Paris officers, and proposed provincial camp become competing security projects.
The Guard is opened to all citizens after the Brunswick threat, displacing the earlier property-based dominance.
Many guards at the Tuileries defect to the Commune's side during the assault.

subjects.label: Longwy and Verdun: invasion panic
subjects.meaning: The rapid fall of frontier positions made traitors seem ubiquitous and created immediate fear that no fortress protected the road to Paris.
subjects.stance: The military news is a trigger for searches and massacres, not evidence that imprisoned suspects actually formed a coordinated plot.

target_labels: Domiciliary visits, mass arrests, and prison overcrowding
September Massacres
Military defeat, treason panic, and domestic radicalization

evidence.evidence_summary: News that Longwy falls with little resistance drives a general search and thousands of arrests.
The danger at Verdun creates panic and immediately precedes the first prison killings.

subjects.label: Battle of Valmy and its political significance
subjects.meaning: French forces halted the Prussians at Valmy, opened negotiations, and achieved a military turn at the moment the Convention met and declared a republic.
subjects.stance: Its world-historical meaning is partly conveyed through a witness's judgment; the secure chapter-level claims are the stopped invasion, negotiations, and political conjunction with the Republic.

target_labels: Longwy and Verdun: invasion panic
Abolition of monarchy and establishment of the Republic

evidence.evidence_summary: French numerical and artillery advantages, combined with patriotic resolve, stop the Prussian advance.
The Prussians negotiate and withdraw as the Convention meets and declares a republic.

subjects.label: Transformation of warfare through patriotic mass participation
subjects.meaning: Popular volunteering and national enthusiasm challenged assumptions about orderly eighteenth-century warfare and helped convert panic into effective resistance.
subjects.stance: The transformation is qualified: Valmy also depended on trained commanders and superior professional artillery, so patriotic energy alone is not the explanation.

target_labels: From massacre panic to patriotic volunteering
Battle of Valmy and its political significance

evidence.evidence_summary: Mass volunteering and battlefield enthusiasm surprise a professional observer and precede the stand at Valmy.
Valmy is interpreted as the beginning of a new historical epoch, while its immediate result is Prussian negotiation.

subjects.label: Saint-Domingue slave uprising and colonial civil war
subjects.meaning: The August 1791 uprising grew into the largest and only successful slave rebellion, embedded in a fast-moving colonial civil war and plantation expansion.
subjects.stance: The source emphasizes both enslaved agency and the destabilizing background of racial conflict and metropolitan incoherence; it does not reduce the revolt to a single decree.

target_labels: Failure of revolutionary colonial policy
Sugar shortage and women's popular price-fixing

evidence.evidence_summary: The uprising's scale, plantation destruction, historical importance, and development into a complex civil war are analyzed.

subjects.label: Failure of revolutionary colonial policy
subjects.meaning: The Constituent Assembly failed to produce coherent policy on slavery, the slave trade, free people of color, and colonial autonomy, worsening conflict in Saint-Domingue and other islands.
subjects.stance: Policy failure is one contributor among plantation growth, racial struggle, and communication delay; it is not presented as the sole cause of revolt.
acceptable_access: rights of free people of color

target_labels: Saint-Domingue slave uprising and colonial civil war

evidence.evidence_summary: Inconsistent metropolitan decisions and a three-month information lag compound racial and political conflict in the colonies.

subjects.label: Bordeaux and Brissotin entanglement with the Caribbean slave economy
subjects.meaning: The uprising embarrassed antislavery Brissot and allied Bordeaux politicians because their port's prosperity was closely tied to Caribbean slavery.
subjects.stance: The point is a political-economic tension, not a claim that every Bordeaux deputy held the same position on slavery.

target_labels: Brissotins/Girondins: war leadership and loss of popular control
Saint-Domingue slave uprising and colonial civil war

evidence.evidence_summary: Brissot's antislavery background and Bordeaux's dependence on the Caribbean economy make the colonial crisis politically awkward for his circle.

subjects.label: Sugar shortage and women's popular price-fixing
subjects.meaning: Colonial disruption tripled sugar prices and prompted largely female crowds to seize sugar and coffee and sell them at older prices.
subjects.stance: The action is popular economic regulation arising from scarcity, not simple looting detached from price claims.

target_labels: Saint-Domingue slave uprising and colonial civil war
Food provisioning and grain riots

evidence.evidence_summary: Severe sugar scarcity reaches Paris and produces organized, predominantly female price-fixing actions in eastern districts.

subjects.label: Food provisioning and grain riots
subjects.meaning: Paris protected its own bread supply by drawing down surrounding reserves, while smaller towns faced grain-price conflict, export resistance, and lethal disorder.
subjects.stance: The chapter links capital provisioning to regional scarcity and unrest rather than treating each riot as an isolated local failure.

target_labels: Paris sections and popular societies
Depreciation of the livre and assignats

evidence.evidence_summary: Parisian stockpiling keeps bread relatively secure but depletes reserves over a wide surrounding area.
Price conflict kills the mayor of Etampes and an attempted export provokes major disorder at Dunkirk.

subjects.label: Depreciation of the livre and assignats
subjects.meaning: Falling exchange value of both monetary instruments raised prices, especially for imports, and intensified popular accusations against merchants and hoarders.
subjects.stance: Currency depreciation compounds scarcity; the source does not treat all price rises as the product of hoarding.

target_labels: Food provisioning and grain riots
Paris sections and popular societies

evidence.evidence_summary: The declining livre and assignat are quantified and connected to rising prices and municipal threats against merchants.

subjects.label: Marseilles: regional radicalism and intervention
subjects.meaning: Marseilles sought regional primacy through armed intervention in Avignon, Aix, and Arles and later supplied politically influential federes to Paris.
subjects.stance: Its activism is presented as both patriotic and destabilizing, not as neutral enforcement of national policy.

target_labels: Arles and the Chiffon counter-revolution
Federes as military volunteers and political actors
The Marseillaise: composition and naming

evidence.evidence_summary: Marseilles intervenes militarily across the department and leads the siege and seizure of Arles.
Its delayed contingent enters Paris singing the Rhine Army hymn and becomes central to federe politics.

subjects.label: Arles and the Chiffon counter-revolution
subjects.meaning: Arles became a regional center of refractory counter-revolution under the Chiffon until a Marseilles-led force captured the city and expelled its leaders.
subjects.stance: The conflict intensified an already polarized south and fed rumors of continuing plots; it was not a self-contained municipal dispute.

target_labels: Marseilles: regional radicalism and intervention
Southern peasant anti-feudal violence

evidence.evidence_summary: The Chiffon controls Arles until a large Marseilles-led force besieges and captures it.
Fear that reactionaries in Arles and Avignon could reverse revolutionary gains helps explain rural action.

subjects.label: Pont-Saint-Esprit drownings as catalyst
subjects.meaning: The drowning of National Guardsmen was widely interpreted as a counter-revolutionary plot and triggered a broad wave of southern rural violence.
subjects.stance: The source reports the conspiratorial interpretation as contemporary belief; it does not affirm that the deaths were deliberately caused.

target_labels: Southern peasant anti-feudal violence

evidence.evidence_summary: The disaster is immediately understood as revenge for patriotic victories and becomes a trigger for attacks.
Belief in a plot sustains fear that counter-revolution might succeed indirectly.

subjects.label: Southern peasant anti-feudal violence
subjects.meaning: Peasants attacked castles, records, symbols, nobles, and nonjurors across the south because they believed the gains of 1789 remained reversible and state authority could not secure them.
subjects.stance: The interpretation emphasizes defense of revolutionary gains amid rumor and weak government, not undirected rural criminality.

target_labels: Pont-Saint-Esprit drownings as catalyst
Arles and the Chiffon counter-revolution
Irreversibility of the destruction of the old order

evidence.evidence_summary: Rumor after the drownings produces attacks on nonjurors, nobles, property, and feudal records.
The geographic spread and anti-feudal targets support an interpretation centered on fear that 1789 could be reversed.

subjects.label: Irreversibility of the destruction of the old order
subjects.meaning: Popular anti-feudal action, war, republican overthrow, and regicide progressively reduced the possibility of restoring the old social and political order.
subjects.stance: Irreversibility is a chapter-level synthesis, not a claim that every institution of the old order vanished at once.

target_labels: Southern peasant anti-feudal violence
Consequences and meaning of regicide

evidence.evidence_summary: Peasants act to make feudal destruction irreversible, and the newly begun war is said to do still more toward that end.
Regicide completes a total political rupture and makes compromise or return far less plausible.

subjects.label: Paris sections and popular societies
subjects.meaning: Neighborhood organizations revived under economic and military pressure, broadened participation, coordinated petitions and armed action, formed a central committee, and seized municipal power.
subjects.stance: The sections became an alternative locus of sovereignty and mobilization; they were numerous and not always unanimous despite later collective claims.

target_labels: Sans-culottes as a political movement
Insurrection of 10 August 1792 and assault on the Tuileries
Insurrectionary Paris Commune

evidence.evidence_summary: Popular societies multiply in eastern and central sections and press for continuous assembly during the emergency.
Sections coordinate the 20 June demonstration and learn from its failure.
Assemblies admit wider participation, sit continuously, and coordinate with federes.
A central committee and deposition petitions move beyond legislative control.
The central committee seizes municipal power as an insurrectionary Commune and directs armed forces.

subjects.label: Sans-culottes as a political movement
subjects.meaning: Ordinary artisans and tradesmen claimed a political identity, drove demonstrations and insurrection, demanded vengeance, participated in massacres, volunteered for war, and pressured representative institutions.
subjects.stance: The movement is socially and politically consequential but not homogeneous; its members' beliefs and actions are explained without endorsing violence.
acceptable_access: artisans and tradesmen in the Revolution

target_labels: Paris sections and popular societies
Insurrection of 10 August 1792 and assault on the Tuileries
September Massacres
From massacre panic to patriotic volunteering

evidence.evidence_summary: Demonstrators publicly adopt the sans-culotte identity while invading the Tuileries and demanding ministerial change.
Sections widen participation to mobilize ordinary citizens for a future confrontation.
Armed citizens and federes coordinate deposition and insurrectionary action.
Shopkeepers, tradesmen, and artisans form much of the force that defeats the palace defense.
Their demand for vengeance and influence over ministry and surveillance shape post-insurrectionary government.
Prison-plot fears and popular justice lead sans-culottes into the first massacre attacks.
Artisans carry out killings they believe necessary, then volunteer for the front in large numbers.
Fear of renewed sans-culotte action forms part of the environment surrounding the king's sentence.

subjects.label: Demonstration of 20 June 1792
subjects.meaning: An armed mass entered the Tuileries to demand restoration of ministers and an end to royal obstruction but failed to intimidate Louis XVI.
subjects.stance: Its immediate failure and the sympathy it generated for the royal family are as important as its precedent for the more decisive August confrontation.

target_labels: Cordeliers-centered popular coordination
Paris sections and popular societies
Insurrection of 10 August 1792 and assault on the Tuileries

evidence.evidence_summary: A large armed procession occupies the palace, confronts the king, and leaves without securing its demands.
The episode's lessons, rather than its immediate outcome, establish the pattern for a decisive second attempt.

subjects.label: Insurrection of 10 August 1792 and assault on the Tuileries
subjects.meaning: Sections, federes, and a democratized Guard overthrew royal authority, defeated the palace defense, suspended monarchy, and shifted effective power to the Commune.
subjects.stance: The event is both a popular revolution and a bloody armed conflict; its decisiveness does not erase internal divisions among former allies.

target_labels: Demonstration of 20 June 1792
Paris sections and popular societies
Brunswick Manifesto and the overthrow of monarchy
Insurrectionary Paris Commune

evidence.evidence_summary: A central committee, federes, and democratized guards prepare direct action as legislative decisions fail.
The Commune seizes power, armed forces attack the Tuileries, the Swiss are defeated, and monarchy is suspended.
The aftermath leaves a rump Assembly governing under Commune pressure.

subjects.label: Swiss Guards and violence of 10 August
subjects.meaning: The Swiss garrison opened fire, was overwhelmed, and suffered extensive killing during retreat and even after supposed safe custody.
subjects.stance: The source records both the guards' initial fire and the disproportionate retaliatory massacre; it does not present all deaths as ordinary combat.

target_labels: Insurrection of 10 August 1792 and assault on the Tuileries
September Massacres

evidence.evidence_summary: The Swiss open fire, retreat, and are pursued and killed in large numbers, including some after the fighting.
Surviving defenders later form one politically identified group among massacre victims.

subjects.label: Insurrectionary Paris Commune
subjects.meaning: The sectional central committee seized municipal power, directed the 10 August forces, dominated the remaining Assembly, pursued vengeance and surveillance, resisted new elections, and coordinated prison killings.
subjects.stance: The Commune is a powerful collective actor, but the text does not make it the sole originator of every popular action or massacre.

target_labels: Paris sections and popular societies
Insurrection of 10 August 1792 and assault on the Tuileries
Legislative Assembly: declining authority and subordination to the Commune

evidence.evidence_summary: The central committee proclaims an insurrectionary Commune and orders the march on the palace.
The Commune dictates much of the rump Assembly's agenda and pursues vengeance and surveillance.
It rejects disbandment, threatens opponents, supervises prisons, and coordinates rather than halts the killings.
It pays perpetrators and becomes a central object of later factional blame.

subjects.label: Suspension of monarchy and confinement in the Temple
subjects.meaning: The fall of the palace ended effective royal authority; the Assembly suspended monarchy and the royal family entered close confinement pending the Convention.
subjects.stance: Suspension was formally provisional, but contemporaries doubted any restoration without foreign victory.

target_labels: Insurrection of 10 August 1792 and assault on the Tuileries
Trial of Louis XVI: legality and procedure

evidence.evidence_summary: The Assembly suspends monarchy and transfers the royal family to the Temple under guard while awaiting a Convention decision.

subjects.label: Political surveillance after 10 August
subjects.meaning: Passports, certificates of civism, sectional committees, clerical arrests, and broad monitoring restricted movement and defined presumed enemies after the overthrow.
subjects.stance: Surveillance grew from genuine invasion danger but operated through expansive and often indiscriminate suspicion.

target_labels: Insurrectionary Paris Commune
Counter-revolution and the enemy within

evidence.evidence_summary: Movement out of Paris requires passports and civic certificates while section vigilantes arrest priests and other suspects.

subjects.label: Special tribunal, guillotine, and revolutionary justice
subjects.meaning: A machine introduced as reliable, humane, and egalitarian became an instrument of political execution, while dissatisfaction with a slow special tribunal encouraged demands for direct popular justice.
subjects.stance: The text distinguishes legal revolutionary punishment from the later makeshift prison tribunals, even as impatience linked them politically.

target_labels: Counter-revolution and the enemy within
Popular justice, acquittals, and perpetrators' motives in the massacres

evidence.evidence_summary: The guillotine is introduced as a mechanical, egalitarian, and supposedly painless method of capital punishment.
A tribunal is established for political crimes and carries out its first political execution.
Commune activists' anger at the tribunal's pace feeds support for prison massacre and improvised courts.

subjects.label: Domiciliary visits, mass arrests, and prison overcrowding
subjects.meaning: The invasion crisis produced a general search of Paris dwellings, thousands of arrests, and prisons filled with presumed traitors.
subjects.stance: The arrests created the setting for prison-plot fears but did not establish that detainees were collectively dangerous.

target_labels: Longwy and Verdun: invasion panic
September Massacres

evidence.evidence_summary: Danton's crisis response orders house searches that add roughly three thousand prisoners to already crowded jails.
Militants fear that the concentrated prison population will threaten families when volunteers leave for the front.

subjects.label: September Massacres
subjects.meaning: Invasion panic, prison-plot beliefs, Commune politics, and improvised tribunals produced the killing of roughly half the Paris prison population over several days.
subjects.stance: The Commune coordinated and encouraged the killings but is not described as their sole origin; most victims were not politically dangerous.

target_labels: Longwy and Verdun: invasion panic
Domiciliary visits, mass arrests, and prison overcrowding
Political memory and blame for the September Massacres

evidence.evidence_summary: Bad news from Verdun precedes attacks on prisoner convoys and prisons, with improvised courts and Commune coordination.
The scale, mixed victim population, perpetrator beliefs, public horror, and long factional afterlife are assessed.

subjects.label: Popular justice, acquittals, and perpetrators' motives in the massacres
subjects.meaning: Makeshift prison courts acquitted many detainees, while ordinary artisans believed killing presumed plotters protected the Revolution and their families.
subjects.stance: The presence of acquittals and sincere belief explains the structure and motivation of violence without legitimating it or proving the alleged conspiracy.

target_labels: September Massacres
Special tribunal, guillotine, and revolutionary justice

evidence.evidence_summary: Improvised courts claim to dispense justice and publicly celebrate acquittals while killings continue.
Tradesmen and artisans believe the purge necessary and beneficial, and the Commune rewards them.

subjects.label: Victims and indiscriminate scope of the September Massacres
subjects.meaning: Victims included Swiss defenders, priests, former elites, and political prisoners, but most were common criminals with no serious counter-revolutionary role.
subjects.stance: Victim categories must preserve the source's corrective emphasis that political danger was not the norm.

target_labels: September Massacres
Counter-revolution and the enemy within

evidence.evidence_summary: The victim profile ranges from identifiable political targets to a majority of ordinary criminals whose offenses were not politically subversive.

subjects.label: Political memory and blame for the September Massacres
subjects.meaning: The massacres horrified observers and became a durable weapon in mutual accusations between Brissotin/Girondin and Robespierrist/Montagnard factions.
subjects.stance: No side's accusation is accepted as a complete causal account; the political label associated with the killings outlived the immediate event.

target_labels: Emergence of the Girondin-Montagnard conflict
September Massacres

evidence.evidence_summary: Public horror, factional charges, an enduring term of abuse, and continuing fear make the killings a long-lived political issue.

subjects.label: From massacre panic to patriotic volunteering
subjects.meaning: Believing internal threats had been removed, Parisian militants volunteered in large numbers and contributed to the mobilization that preceded Valmy.
subjects.stance: The source describes the militants' sense of reassurance and the sequence into volunteering; it does not morally validate the killings as necessary.

target_labels: September Massacres
Transformation of warfare through patriotic mass participation
Battle of Valmy and its political significance

evidence.evidence_summary: Large numbers volunteer once militants believe their families no longer face a prison conspiracy.
Valmy turns the resulting mobilization into a decisive halt to invasion.

subjects.label: The Marseillaise: composition and naming
subjects.meaning: Rouget de Lisle composed a Rhine Army battle hymn during the first war enthusiasm; it acquired its enduring name when Marseilles volunteers entered Paris singing it.
subjects.stance: The hymn expresses militant patriotic defiance and is not treated as a neutral ceremonial song.

target_labels: Revolutionary internationalism and liberation war
Federes as military volunteers and political actors

evidence.evidence_summary: The battle hymn is composed for the Rhine Army and conveys the violent defiance of early war enthusiasm.
Marseilles volunteers bring the song into Paris and give it the name by which it becomes known.

subjects.label: The guillotine's introduction
subjects.meaning: Retention of capital punishment led to a mechanical decapitation method presented as reliable, egalitarian, and humane before it became political machinery.
subjects.stance: The text explicitly distinguishes Guillotin's original proposal from actual invention of the device.

target_labels: Special tribunal, guillotine, and revolutionary justice

evidence.evidence_summary: The device's rationale, disputed attribution, and first ordinary criminal execution are explained.

subjects.label: Revolutionary anniversaries and the journee model
subjects.meaning: Anniversaries, liberty-tree rituals, the 14 July festival, the tocsin, and memories of 1789 supplied symbols and scripts for popular mobilization.
subjects.stance: Ceremonial continuity did not imply political consensus; official festivals could appear empty to militants preparing insurrection.

target_labels: Demonstration of 20 June 1792
Insurrection of 10 August 1792 and assault on the Tuileries

evidence.evidence_summary: The June action uses the Tennis Court anniversary and liberty-tree planting as its public occasion.
The 14 July festival mobilizes federes but is judged emotionally hollow by radicals preparing a new Bastille-like assault.
The tocsin and remembered popular days of 1789 provide the signal and model for insurrection.

subjects.label: Revolutionary calendar and Year I
subjects.meaning: The later revolutionary calendar dated Year I from the Republic's foundation in September 1792, formalizing the break with monarchy.
subjects.stance: The calendar is retrospective institutionalization of the republican rupture, not an event that caused the September declaration.

target_labels: Abolition of monarchy and establishment of the Republic

evidence.evidence_summary: The calendar is said to begin from the first day of the Republic following abolition of monarchy.

exclusions.label: Attribution-only local speakers and officials
exclusions.reason: Couthon, Isnard, Count d'Antraigues, the mayor of Etampes, and the unnamed murdered general support larger subjects but receive no sustained independent analysis in this chunk.

exclusions.label: Secondary ministers and factional associates as separate subjects
exclusions.reason: Servan, Claviere, Narbonne, Guadet, Gensonne, and Vergniaud are accessible through the Roland ministry, Brissotins/Girondins, war politics, or trial subjects; isolated separate records would duplicate access.

exclusions.label: One-passage radical personalities
exclusions.reason: Clootz, Chaumette, and Jacques Roux are useful names within internationalist or popular-radical evidence, but separate absence would not materially reduce chapter retrieval.

exclusions.label: Convention election examples
exclusions.reason: Orleans/Philippe-Egalite, Paine, and Priestley illustrate the Convention's composition and international associations but are not independently analyzed here.

exclusions.label: Louis XVI's counsel as an independent subject
exclusions.reason: Raymond de Seze and the defense speech are evidence within the trial; the chapter does not sustain a separate analysis of counsel.

exclusions.label: Named observers and quoted witnesses
exclusions.reason: The English visitor, American ambassador, British agent, and Goethe supply perspective or interpretation rather than independently treated subjects.

exclusions.label: German electors as separate subjects
exclusions.reason: Trier and Mainz are elements in the emigre and war-origin sequence; the chapter does not independently analyze either polity.

exclusions.label: Neighboring-chapter military expansion
exclusions.reason: The post-Valmy conquests and military recovery discussion on context pages 197-198 belong to CHUNK-009 ownership.

exclusions.label: Polish crisis of 1792
exclusions.reason: The Targowica, Kosciuszko, and partition material occurs on context page 198 and belongs to the next chunk.

exclusions.label: Dates, casualty figures, and vote totals as standalone subjects
exclusions.reason: They remain important attributes and evidence within events but do not create independent concepts.

exclusions.label: Running furniture and note markers
exclusions.reason: Running heads, page numbers, chapter numerals, and superscript note markers are not substantive source matter.

exclusions.label: Absent notes and endnotes
exclusions.reason: The supplied PDF omits their text, so they are unavailable and excluded rather than treated as omissions.

uncertainties.item: Historical staging of Brissotin and Girondin terminology
alternatives: Use Brissotins for the earlier war group and Girondins/Gironde faction only as the conflict coheres
Use a combined access label with an explicit chronology note
uncertainties.evidence_needed: Whole-book synthesis should confirm preferred terminology and cross-chapter identity continuity.

alternatives: Index as an alleged conspiracy
Route through Marie Antoinette's secret correspondence with a qualification
uncertainties.evidence_needed: No further source evidence is required for this chunk; whole-book synthesis should preserve the distinction between rumor and actual correspondence.

uncertainties.item: Commune responsibility for the September Massacres
alternatives: Coordination and encouragement
Central direction of all killings
uncertainties.evidence_needed: Retain the chapter's narrower claim that the Commune coordinated rather than stopped the killings; do not infer a single comprehensive order.

uncertainties.item: Perpetrators' belief and the political status of massacre victims
alternatives: Popular defense against a believed prison plot
Actual elimination of a largely counter-revolutionary prisoner body
uncertainties.evidence_needed: Keep both perpetrator belief and the source's conclusion that most victims were not politically dangerous.

uncertainties.item: Causal link from the massacres to volunteering
alternatives: Perceived internal security released volunteers
The massacres objectively made volunteering safe
uncertainties.evidence_needed: Use the first, source-grounded formulation and avoid moral or causal overstatement.

uncertainties.item: Effect of sans-culotte pressure on the king's death vote
alternatives: Fear perhaps influenced some deputies
Coercion determined the sentence
uncertainties.evidence_needed: Preserve the author's qualified modal claim and the independently recorded vote divisions.

uncertainties.item: War and the irreversibility of anti-feudal change
alternatives: War reinforced and secured the destruction of the old order
War alone caused the southern attacks
uncertainties.evidence_needed: Use the reinforcing relationship; the attacks also arose from local polarization, rumor, and weak government.

alternatives: A new epoch as reported through Goethe
A military and political turning point directly supported by the chapter narrative
uncertainties.evidence_needed: Use the second as the principal stance and retain the first as attributed contemporary interpretation.

uncertainties.item: Priority of the Saint-Domingue material within this chapter
alternatives: Major localized subject
Essential chapter subject
uncertainties.evidence_needed: Whole-book synthesis should decide global priority; the chunk assigns major because the material is consequential but not the chapter's organizing center.

alternatives: Optional named catalyst
Evidence only within southern rural violence
uncertainties.evidence_needed: Whole-book synthesis should determine whether the named event warrants direct access beyond the major regional subject.

uncertainties.item: Chunk boundary around Valmy and post-Valmy war
alternatives: Own Valmy through page 193
Transfer post-battle military explanation to the next chapter
uncertainties.evidence_needed: The frozen manifest owns pages 174-196 here; pages 197-198 were used only as context. Valmy evidence is therefore limited to owned pages 192-193.
